title: Security Opportunities and Challenges for Disaggregated Architectures (Invited)
problem: Disaggregated computer architectures separate CPU, memory, storage, and networking into independently managed units communicating over networks, introducing new security attack surfaces and isolation risks.
motivation: Disaggregation offers flexibility, scalability, and resource optimization benefits, but unique security challenges require systematic analysis for O-RAN and enterprise systems.
method: This paper examines the security risks that come from breaking computer systems into separate, independent pieces (CPU, memory, storage, networking) connected by networks. The authors look at three real-world contexts: enterprise networks where data travels between separate routers (network fabric), systems that manage radio signals through software (O-RAN), and hardware designed to run trusted code safely (trusted execution environments). They identify the new attack points that appear when pieces are separate—such as data getting exposed during network transfer, losing track of where data came from (provenance), systems not being properly isolated from each other, and problems with how different parts communicate through APIs.
key_novelty: This paper examines the security threats and opportunities that come from breaking computer systems into separate networked pieces, focusing on radio systems controlled by software (O-RAN).
contributions: Framework for analyzing security in disaggregated systems
Discussion of increased attack surfaces from network communication
Data provenance tracking challenges in disaggregated architectures
Redesign requirements for TEEs in disaggregated contexts
Application to enterprise routing, O-RAN, and network infrastructure
limitations: Invited position paper; focuses on analysis rather than proposing concrete solutions.
primary_theme: Security implications of disaggregated computing architectures
